c1.story:
Flip a light switch in Bengaluru and the electricity that answers has passed through more machines than you would guess. A turbine spun it, a generator made it, a step-up transformer pushed it onto a high-voltage line, switchgear protected it at a dozen substations, a distribution transformer stepped it down, and a copper cable carried it into your wall. Every one of those boxes was built by a capital goods company. This is the industry that makes the machines that make everything else.

That sounds like one business. It is at least four, and they behave so differently that lumping them together is the most common mistake investors make here.

The first door sells equipment off a waiting list. ABB India, Siemens, Hitachi Energy and GE Vernova's Indian arm make transformers, switchgear, motors and drives, product by product, and right now the whole world is short of transformers. When the customer is queuing, the seller sets the price. The second door builds entire plants to order. Larsen and Toubro and BHEL agree a price for a refinery, a power station or a metro line, then spend years building it while copper, steel and wages move under their feet. The third door, Polycab, Havells and APAR, turns copper and aluminium into wire and cable by the kilometre, with the metal price written into the invoice. The fourth door, Cummins, Bharat Forge and Solar Industries, makes the parts and consumables that go into other people's machines and mines: gensets, crankshafts, explosives.

Same capex headline, four different stocks. The door decides what the news means.

Here is why it matters. A big transmission tender is pure good news for the first door, which gets orders at firm prices. It is mixed news for the second, which gets work but at a price competed down in a tender. It is volume news for the third. And it barely registers for the fourth, which watches truck exports to America and coal output instead.

Many companies straddle doors. L&T sells equipment, builds projects and runs a technology services arm on the side; Bharat Forge sells crankshafts to truck makers and artillery shells to the army. Value the pieces separately in your head, because the market reprices each one at a different moment in the cycle.
c1.read:
Four tiles, four doors. Read each tile top to bottom.

  • The name and the line under it tell you how the money arrives: product by product off an order book, in milestones over years, by the kilometre with metal passed through, or as parts sold into someone else's machine.
  • The tickers are listed names that mostly sit behind that door. Click one to open its stock page. Notice that the grid door is crowded with Indian arms of multinationals, ABB, Siemens, Hitachi Energy and GE Vernova, while the project door is home-grown: L&T and BHEL.
  • The profit bar is the part to stare at. Grid and power equipment sits at the high end, because a shortage of transformer capacity lets makers hold prices. Project builders sit at the low end, because they win work by bidding lowest and carry the cost risk for years. Cables and engines sit in the middle: real brands and real niches, but with metal or export customers taking a share.
  • The last line is the bet you are actually making. Read it twice for the project door: a bet on execution without cost overruns is a bet on things not going wrong.

A useful drill: take any capital goods name in your portfolio and ask which tile it belongs to, and whether the market is paying it a first-door multiple for a second-door business. That mismatch is where most disappointments in this sector start.

Below the tiles, the analogy of sewing machines, garment factories, thread and motors is the short version to remember.

c2.story:
Picture a long workshop with five stations. Metal comes in at one end. At the other, a utility engineer signs a delivery note for a working substation. Everything in between is where capital goods companies earn or lose their money.

Station one is metal: copper, aluminium, steel plate and one awkward ingredient most investors have never heard of, cold-rolled grain-oriented electrical steel. That is the special steel stacked inside every transformer core, engineered so magnetism flows through it with as little loss as possible. India barely makes it. It comes from Japan, Korea and China, and in a global transformer boom it is rationed. A transformer built in Vadodara therefore begins its life on a ship from Asia.

Station two turns metal into parts: crankshafts, castings, windings, bushings, insulators. Bharat Forge in Pune is the famous name, but behind it stand hundreds of mid-size machine shops in Rajkot, Coimbatore and Faridabad, the unglamorous base the whole industry rests on.

Station three is assembly, where parts become a transformer, a switchgear panel, a motor or a genset. This is where the multinationals' Indian arms live, along with CG Power, Cummins and BHEL. CG Power is a good reminder that this station can be rebuilt: after its old management's accounting fraud came to light in 2019, the Murugappa group's Tube Investments took control in 2020 and turned it into one of the sector's cleanest stories.

Station four is integration: engineering the equipment into a working plant, line or factory and commissioning it on site. L&T and BHEL dominate here, along with the transmission contractors. Station five is the buyer, usually a utility, a PSU or the railways, who takes delivery and pays over years.

The shortage sits at station three. The tender sits at station four. That one step explains the margin gap.

And China? Chinese makers stand at station three with cheaper transformers and turbines, and they once won plenty of Indian power-plant orders. Since 2020, procurement rules have largely kept them out of Indian grid and PSU tenders, which is why the rival band in this kitchen is more threat than presence.
c2.read:
Two layers: the five station boxes on top, the bands underneath. Read the boxes left to right first.

The five boxes run from raw metal on the left to the paying customer on the right. Under each name you get what happens there and who stands there. Watch the names change as you move right: metal makers and Japanese mills, then forging shops, then the equipment brands, then the big project houses, and finally Power Grid, NTPC, the railways and the data-centre developers.

The first band row labels who holds each station. Here the Indian listed band covers three stations in a row, two, three and four, which is unusual. In many industries listed India sits in one narrow slot; in capital goods it owns the whole middle of the workshop. The left band, metal makers and Japan, is the dependency; the right band, utilities and PSUs, is the customer who sets payment terms.

The second band row shows where China stands. Look at how it lines up against station three, assembly, where Chinese transformers and turbines are cheaper. The note on station four is the telling detail: Chinese EPC firms compete overseas, not in India.

Then read the geography note. The heavy electrical clusters around Vadodara, Bengaluru, Nashik and Bhopal matter less than the one input India does not make: transformer steel.

Use the diagram as a shock tracer. A Japanese steel mill rationing supply at station one lands as a delay at station three. A utility slowing payments at station five lands as receivables at station four. The so-what line underneath names the key contrast: a seller's market at station three, a price taker at station four.

c3.story:
Nobody buys a transformer because they like transformers. They buy one because a solar park in Rajasthan needs to send its power to Mumbai, or because a data centre in Navi Mumbai needs a substation of its own, or because the railways are electrifying another stretch of track. Capital goods demand is always somebody else's plan made physical.

That makes the customer list the single best forecasting tool you have. And right now it is unusually lopsided.

The loudest buyer is the grid. India has committed to five hundred gigawatts of non-fossil capacity by 2030, and a solar farm is worthless until a transmission line connects it. Every new renewable auction therefore drags a trail of transformer, switchgear and conductor orders behind it, a year or so later. Power Grid and the state transmission companies have been ordering at a pace not seen in more than a decade.

Power generation has quietly come back too. After years when nobody would touch a coal plant, peak-demand shortfalls pushed NTPC and state utilities to order new thermal capacity, and BHEL's order book swelled with boilers and turbines it had not sold in volume since the early 2010s. The railways, with electrification, Vande Bharat trains and freight corridors, remain a steady budget-driven buyer.

Then come the buyers who move with the private economy: real estate for wires, fans and switches; factories for motors, drives and automation; refiners for process equipment; and miners for explosives. Data centres are the new face in the queue, hungry for power gear and cooling.

The government is ordering. The grid is ordering. The private factory owner is still thinking about it.

That last point is the swing factor. Private industrial capex has been patchy, held back by global uncertainty and, in 2025, by steep US tariffs on Indian goods. If factory owners join the utilities, a good cycle becomes a long one. If they do not, the cycle depends on how long the state keeps writing cheques.
c3.read:
Eight tiles, one per customer group. Each tile reads in three lines.

  • The name is the buyer.
  • What it buys tells you which door benefits: transformers and switchgear point to the grid door; boilers and turbines to BHEL and L&T; wires and fans to the cables door; explosives and forgings to the components door.
  • What moves it is your watch list outside the sector. Power Grid capex plans, renewable auctions, the railway budget, housing launches, private capex confidence, coal output.

Now sort the tiles into two piles. Pile one is state-directed: transmission, generation, railways, and mostly oil and gas, which is PSU refiners. Pile two is market-directed: real estate, private factories, and mining and defence through their own cycles. Today pile one is doing the heavy lifting, which the so-what line beneath the grid says plainly: grid and renewables are ordering, private factories have not fully shown up.

Then link each tile back to a door from the first card. A company whose book leans on transmission and renewables is riding the strongest tile. A company leaning on private factories is waiting for the swing buyer. A company leaning on US truck exports, a forging name for instance, is reading a tile outside India altogether.

The best use of this grid is during a results season. Before a capital goods company reports, read the commentary of its biggest customer tile. Power Grid's capex guidance, a housing developer's completions or Coal India's volumes tell you about the supplier's next quarter before the supplier does.

c4.story:
Here is a puzzle. Two companies sit in the same industry, sell to the same utilities and ride the same capex boom. One keeps a healthy slice of every rupee it bills. The other keeps a sliver and occasionally reports a loss on a contract that looked fine two years earlier. Why?

The answer is the shape of the promise each one makes. An equipment maker sells a transformer at a price agreed today for delivery in months. If copper jumps, it can usually reprice the next order, and in a shortage it can add a premium for a delivery slot. A project builder promises a whole plant at a fixed price for delivery in years. Steel, cement, copper and wages can all move against it, and a stuck site can stretch a two-year job into four.

That shows up first in the raw-material line. The project builder passes most of every rupee straight through to suppliers and sub-contractors, so a small cost slip eats a big share of what remains. The equipment maker spends more on people, design and testing, the price of being a product company, but keeps far more at the bottom.

An equipment maker is paid for scarcity. A project builder is paid for taking risk, and sometimes the risk wins.

Then there are the lines a newcomer misses. The order book is not on the P&L at all, yet it is the P&L of two years from now and the market reads it first. Working capital is where project builders bleed: retention money held back until a project is accepted, unbilled work, and state utilities that pay late. And other income can be surprisingly large, because customer advances sit as cash and earn interest. Part of a big contractor's reported profit can be treasury income rather than engineering.

Depreciation, the line that dominates chemicals or steel, barely matters here. Assembly halls are cheap next to the sales they carry, which is why the best equipment makers earn returns on capital that look almost like a software company's.
c4.read:
Two bar charts, each walking a hundred rupees of sales down to what is left. The left is grid and power equipment; the right is the project builders. Move left to right in each.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees of sales.
  • The input bar, raw materials and components, is the big bite. For the equipment maker it takes a little under three fifths. For the project builder it takes nearly three quarters. Look at that gap: it is the margin story before anything else happens.
  • The opex bar, people, power, freight and site costs, is a bit larger for the equipment maker, which spends on engineers, design and type testing.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is a thin sliver in both charts and roughly the same size. Plants are cheap here; this is not where the difference lives.
  • The last bar is what is left. The equipment maker keeps roughly a sixth of sales; the project builder keeps a small fraction of that, and one stuck contract can wipe it out.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover a bar to see the amount.

The list below marks which lines matter. Order inflow, gross margin, working capital and provisions for cost overruns all get a firm yes; notice that two of those four are not even profit lines, they are about cash and risk. Depreciation gets a no. Capex, interest and other income get a sometimes, each with a specific exception: transformer capacity builds, leveraged builders and treasury income on advances.

The so-what tells you the reading order: order inflow against sales first, then gross margin to see whether the book is worth having.

c5.story:
Capital goods cycles are long enough to end careers. If you joined a brokerage's capital goods desk in 2004, you spent four years being right about everything. If you joined in 2012, you spent most of a decade explaining why the turn was coming next year.

The last boom ran from 2004 to 2008. India was ordering power plants, highways and factories all at once; order books tripled and BHEL became one of the most valuable companies in the country. At the peak, private power developers borrowed heavily and bought cheaper boilers and turbines from Chinese makers, while Indian makers added capacity at the top. You can guess what followed.

The bust began in 2012 and lasted most of the decade. Power projects were stranded without coal or buyers, the loans behind them went bad, banks stopped lending and private capex simply disappeared. BHEL's profit collapsed and its order book shrank year after year. Covid in 2020 was the final insult, and for a while the sector traded as if capex would never return.

It did, and from an unexpected direction. Government capex rose with almost every budget from 2021. Transmission tenders appeared to connect renewable farms. Then, around 2023, the grid build-out became a global story. American and European utilities, rebuilding ageing grids and connecting renewables and data centres, found that nobody had added transformer capacity in a decade. Lead times stretched to years, and the Indian arms of ABB, Siemens, Hitachi Energy and GE Vernova re-rated hard.

The order book tells you about demand. The margin tells you how much of that demand you keep. In 2026 both are rising.

By 2026 the cycle has moved from orders to earnings. Old low-price contracts from the lean years have rolled off, new ones carry shortage pricing, and BHEL's quarterly profit has more than doubled. The debate has shifted from whether demand exists to whether valuations already assume it will last.
c5.read:
Three parts: the clock, the timeline beside it, and four hands below.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. The years under each arc belong to the last full cycle, and they show how long it is: a boom from 2004 to 2008, a peak to 2011, a bust that ran from 2012 to 2019, a bottom in 2020. The arrow points into the boom arc, labelled mid-cycle boom: grid orders strong, private capex lagging. Hover an arc for what defined it.

The timeline runs from 2019 to now. The colours tell the story at a glance: two bust years, two boom entries for 2021 to 2023, neutral entries for the 2024 election pause and the patchy 2025, and the now entry for 2026, where results confirm the earnings phase.

The four hands are what moves the arrow.

  • Order inflow growth: strong but decelerating, arrow up. Slowing inflow on a full book is the first whiff of late cycle; watch it every quarter.
  • Transformer and switchgear delivery times: still stretched, arrow up. This is the pricing-power gauge. When lead times shorten, grid-door margins have peaked.
  • Private capex announcements: patchy, a mixed reading. If they firm up, the cycle lengthens by years.
  • Central government capex: high but growing more slowly, flat. The state is handing the baton to utilities and, it hopes, the private sector.

Read the hands together: two pointing up on demand and pricing, one flat on the state and one mixed on private industry. That is exactly what mid-cycle looks like. The so-what line adds the investing point: the money is in books still growing faster than sales.

c6.story:
Who really decides a capital goods company's results? Not its chief executive, mostly. The finance minister writing the capital outlay into the budget, the grid planner at the Central Electricity Authority drawing next decade's transmission lines, the copper trader in London and the peak-demand number on a hot May afternoon in Delhi have more say than anyone in the boardroom.

Two dials tower over the rest. The first is government and PSU capex, which fills order books roughly a year ahead. Railways, highways and the grid all flow from it. The second is power demand, and especially the gap between peak demand and what the grid can supply. A summer of shortfalls is the most persuasive argument there is for a new thermal plant or another transmission corridor, and India has had several such summers recently.

Then come the two-faced dials. Copper is the biggest input for cables, transformers and motors. For a cable maker it is mostly a pass-through, written into the price, so a rise can even flatter revenue. For an equipment maker or a project builder working on a fixed-price order, a copper spike between quote and delivery comes straight out of margin. The rupee works the same way: a weaker rupee raises the cost of imported transformer steel but helps the forging and engine exporters.

Interest rates are the brake on the private half of the cycle. When money is dear, factory owners delay expansions and leveraged project developers stall. Real estate is the volume dial for the electricals door, because wires and switches are bought at completion.

Government capex fills the book. Power demand makes it urgent. Everything else adjusts the margin.

Finally, the market's own mood sits on the panel too. Infrastructure sentiment can re-rate the whole capex chain before a single extra rupee of earnings arrives, which is both how these stocks get ahead of themselves and how they fall when the mood turns.
c6.read:
One row per dial. Read across each row in order.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: the route by which it reaches profits. This is the column that turns macro news into a question for the next results call.
  • A rise does: a green up arrow helps the industry, a red down arrow hurts, a diamond cuts both ways. Here government capex, power demand, real estate and infrastructure sentiment are green. Interest rates, steel and aluminium, and US and European tariffs are red. Copper, the rupee and crude are diamonds, because they help one door and hurt another.
  • Weight: one to three dots. Only two rows carry three dots, government capex and power demand.

The last column shows today's reading where the dial maps to a series we track: the capital goods output index for capex, electricity output for power demand, the money-market rate, copper, steel output, the rupee, Brent crude, the realty and infrastructure indices, and exports for the tariff row.

How to use it: start with the two three-dot rows and check whether both are still rising; together they decide how long the ordering wave lasts. Then scan the diamonds and ask which door your company sits behind. A copper spike reads as a nuisance for Polycab, which passes it through, and as a margin hit for a project builder halfway through a fixed-price job. The red tariff row matters almost only for the components door, where forging and engine exports go to America and Europe.

The so-what beneath the table says the same thing in one line: track government capex and power demand above all.

c7.story:
If demand is this strong, why can't the industry simply build more and sell more? Because the bottlenecks are real, and oddly, some of them are the reason the best companies are earning so much.

Start with the strangest one. A transformer needs a core of special electrical steel, and India barely makes it. Supply comes from a handful of mills in Japan, Korea and China, and in a global shortage they ration it. That caps how fast Indian transformer makers can grow. It also means no new entrant can flood the market overnight.

The second bottleneck is the transformer shortage itself. Large power transformers take a long time to build and test, and through the long bust nobody added capacity. Now that every utility in the world wants them at once, incumbents enjoy waiting lists and firm prices. For the utility it is a headache; for the shareholder of an incumbent it is the best kind of problem.

The grid door's bottlenecks are its moat. The project door's bottlenecks are its margin.

Now flip to the project builders. Their bottlenecks all cost money. Fixed-price contracts mean that when metal or wages spike, the contractor pays. State power distribution companies, chronically cash-strapped, pay late, so the contractor ends up quietly financing the government. Transmission lines and plants wait years for land and forest clearances, which means an order won is not an order billed. And the calendar bites too: government ordering pauses for a couple of quarters around a general election, as it did in 2024, and slows at the start of every fiscal year.

Chinese competition is the bottleneck that never goes away. Chinese makers are cheaper on boilers, turbines, solar gear and now transformers. India keeps them out with duties and procurement rules rather than by beating them on cost, so a policy change could open the door again. And in a country building everything at once, certified welders and site supervisors are in short supply everywhere, a slow squeeze rather than a sudden one.
c7.read:
Each row is one bottleneck: what it is, why it bites, and a severity label. The label tells you where the risk belongs in your thinking.

  • Structural means permanent: transformer-steel imports, late payments from state utilities and Chinese price competition. These cap returns for the whole cycle, so they belong in your valuation rather than your news feed.
  • Cyclical here is a single row, the transformer shortage. It is unusual because it helps incumbents while it lasts. When the label eventually changes to a glut, grid margins will be the first casualty.
  • Recurring marks the risks that come back: fixed-price contracts biting on a metal spike, land and right-of-way delays, and the election and budget calendar. These move individual stocks for a quarter.
  • Slow is the shortage of skilled engineers and welders, a gradual cost creep across every site.

Now apply the so-what line beneath the table. The first two rows, steel imports and the transformer shortage, explain why the grid door earns record margins: scarcity on both the input and the output side keeps newcomers out. The next three, fixed-price contracts, late utility payments and land delays, explain why the project door does not.

A practical habit: for any project builder you own, read the receivables note and the order-book ageing in the annual report. That is where the recurring rows on this table show up first, often a year before a provision hits the profit line.

c8.story:
In capital goods, the order book is written in Delhi long before it is written in a company's results. The Ministry of Power and the Central Electricity Authority draw up the national transmission plan and the generation targets. That single set of documents decides the size of the biggest order pipeline in the sector, years in advance.

But a plan is only a wish until someone pays for it. That is where the electricity regulators come in. CERC and the state commissions approve how much of its capex a utility can recover from consumers through tariffs. A utility does not order a transformer it cannot bill for, so a regulator's approval is the quiet step between a plan and a purchase order.

The most valuable rule for listed makers is a protectionist one. In July 2020, weeks after the Galwan clash, India restricted bidders from countries sharing a land border from government tenders unless they registered and were cleared. Combined with Make in India purchase preferences, it effectively kept Chinese equipment out of grid and PSU tenders. That rule is a big reason Indian transformer prices have held while Chinese makers sit on spare capacity.

The cheapest transformer in the world is Chinese. The cheapest one a state utility is allowed to buy is not.

Other rules work the same way by other names. BIS quality control orders require imported cables, motors and components to meet Indian standards, a tariff in all but name. The approved list of models and manufacturers for solar steers government-backed projects to Indian module plants. Production-linked incentive schemes pay companies to build factories, and every factory is an order for motors, drives and automation.

Looking ahead, energy-efficiency standards for motors and transformers are the sleeper. When a rule retires inefficient old equipment, it creates replacement demand even if nobody builds a new plant. And abroad, US and EU tariffs on steel products and components are the live threat to the forging and engine exporters.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who it is, what it does, why you care, and its status.

The status column is how to prioritise.

  • Always: the Ministry of Power with the CEA, CERC and the state regulators, and the Railway Board. These are the permanent architecture of demand. They rarely make headlines, but a revised transmission plan or a railway budget is a direct read on the order pipeline.
  • Live: the rules shaping prices and orders today. Public procurement preference and the restricted-country rule, BIS quality control orders, production-linked incentives and the solar approved list all protect domestic makers. The US and EU tariff actions are the one live row that hurts rather than helps.
  • Coming: energy-efficiency rules for motors and transformers. Replacement demand is the slow-burn upside.

Notice the pattern: of the live rows, four are shields against imports and one is a tariff aimed at Indian exports. The domestic order book is heavily protected; the export business is exposed. That asymmetry is worth remembering when you compare a grid name selling mostly at home with a forging name selling mostly to America.

Then look at the why column for the CERC row: a utility can only order what the regulator lets it recover. When you hear about a state utility's finances or a tariff order, that is capital goods news.

Dated regulatory headlines for this industry, filtered from our feed, sit on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Michael Porter's five forces boil down to one question: once the money comes in, who gets to keep it? Suppliers can raise input prices, customers can push down selling prices, rivals can start a price war, newcomers can crowd in, and substitutes can make you unnecessary. Run the two biggest doors in capital goods through that test and you get almost mirror images.

Start with the grid equipment makers. There are only three or four serious makers of large power transformers in India, and their books are full. Rivalry is mild because nobody needs to cut price to win work. Customers, normally powerful utilities, are in a hurry and accept price rises to secure a delivery slot. Entry is hard: a new maker needs type tests, a reference list of installed units and years of track record before a utility trusts it with a critical substation. And substitutes barely exist. Nothing replaces a transformer.

The one force that bites the grid door is suppliers. Transformer steel comes from a few foreign mills that set their own schedules and ration supply. That is the weak spot in an otherwise excellent position.

A utility in a hurry is a price taker. The same utility running a tender is a price setter.

Now the project builders. Rivalry is fierce, with dozens of contractors bidding the lowest price on every tender. The buyer is the same utility, but in a tender it holds all the cards: it sets the terms, the penalties and the payment schedule. New engineering and construction firms appear every cycle. Even the substitute force is non-zero, since a customer can split a project into packages or execute it in-house instead of hiring a single builder.

The result is the pattern you saw on the first card: equipment keeps most of the profit in this cycle because the shortage belongs to it, and project builders keep little and give some back whenever a contract goes wrong.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure that force exerts, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: grid and power equipment, and project builders. Look at the overall size first. The project builders' shape is visibly larger, reaching the outer ring on rivalry and buyer power. The equipment shape is compact, pulled in tight on entrants and substitutes.

Then look for the spoke where the shapes cross. On suppliers, the equipment maker reaches further than the project builder. That is the transformer-steel point from the story: a few foreign mills ration the core ingredient, while for builders metal is closer to a pass-through cost.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero, no pressure, to three, heavy pressure, with a reason.

  • Rivalry: one and a half against three. A small club with full books versus a crowd bidding lowest price.
  • Buyer: one and a half against three, the same utilities behaving differently in a shortage and in a tender.
  • Entrants: one against two. Type testing and reference lists keep equipment makers safe.
  • Substitutes: half against one. Nothing replaces a transformer.

If you think the transformer shortage will end in two years, mentally push the equipment shape outward on rivalry and buyer power and see how much of the advantage survives. That is how to use the radar: not as a verdict, but as a picture you redraw when the facts change.

c10.story:
A capital goods results call can be an hour of plant names, kilovolt ratings and project milestones. Most of it is colour. Eight numbers tell you whether the cycle is still working for the company, and you can check them in the time it takes your tea to cool.

Start with the two order numbers, because the market does. Order inflow growth tells you whether the book is still filling; two quarters of decline at a large name is the first late-cycle sign. Order book to trailing sales tells you how many years of work are already visible. When that ratio falls, sales are eating the book faster than new orders refill it, which is fine for a year and worrying for two.

Then the margin pair. EBITDA margin combines pricing power and execution. Gross margin is the finer tool: it tells you whether copper and steel moves are being passed on. A gross margin that holds steady while copper swings is a company with pricing power or good contract clauses.

Next, receivable days, which tell you who is paying late. For a project builder this is the honest number, because profit on a contract is meaningless until the state utility actually pays.

Orders are a promise. Sales are delivery. Receivables tell you whether anyone paid.

Sales growth tells you whether the book is converting into revenue; a huge book with slow sales means execution, not demand, is the constraint. Return on capital tells you whether all this growth earns its keep. And capex to depreciation, the last row, asks the most forward-looking question: are transformer makers adding capacity into the shortage, or coasting on it? A maker that is not expanding enjoys fat margins today and cedes share tomorrow.
c10.read:
One row per number. Read across: the metric, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask of each company you own.
  • What good looks like holds the only figures on the card. They are rules of thumb that differ by door: notice how the order book, EBITDA margin, receivable days and ROCE rows each give one benchmark for equipment makers and a different one for project builders. Always judge a company against its own door's benchmark.
  • Today's industry median comes from the latest annual filings of the listed companies in our database. Two rows, order inflow growth and order book to sales, have no median because they come from company presentations, not filings; you read those from the results deck.

A good order of reading: first the two order rows from the company's presentation, then gross and EBITDA margin from the results, then receivable days from the balance sheet. That sequence tells you demand, pricing and cash in three steps.

Then the comparison trick. Put three things side by side for any company: its own number, the industry median and the good mark. Because the median blends equipment makers and builders, it will often sit between the two door benchmarks. An equipment maker sitting only at the median is underperforming its door, not matching it.

Finally, pay attention to the last row. Capex to depreciation near one at a transformer maker during a shortage is a quiet warning that management expects the shortage to end, or is leaving share on the table.

c11.story:
Capital goods is the rare industry that hands you its future in writing. A transmission line awarded today is a transformer order in two quarters and revenue in a year. A budget passed in February decides which railway and power orders get placed through the year. The trick is to read the documents that come before the results.

The earliest voice is power demand. A summer of peak shortfalls pushes the government toward new generation and grid approvals, which become orders about three quarters later. Next come the transmission tender awards, Power Grid's capex guidance and the Union budget's capital outlay, each speaking about two quarters ahead. Bank credit to industry and private capex announcements tell you whether factories are about to order motors and drives.

Closer in, copper and steel prices hit next quarter's gross margin on fixed-price orders, global transformer lead times tell you whether pricing power is intact, and housing completions drive cable and switchgear sales. Coal and mineral output moves explosives demand the very same quarter.

Read the tender awards and the budget. The results are just the receipt.

Combine them and you get the three-sign rule. The industry is in a true up-cycle when order inflows outgrow sales, equipment lead times are long, and private capex is joining public capex. All three means boom; two means mid-cycle; one means the book is running down. Today two signs are on: inflows still outgrow sales, though more slowly, and transformers are still rationed. The missing sign is private capex, which remains patchy and clouded by tariffs.

That is why the call favours grid equipment and electricals names with growing books over the project builders, and why it insists on being choosy about valuation. In a mid-cycle boom, the demand is real but the price you pay for it already assumes a lot.

The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for the channel through which it reaches earnings.

Here the dots are spread unusually wide. On the far left, coal and mineral output moves the same quarter. A cluster at one quarter holds copper and steel prices, global transformer lead times and housing completions. At two quarters sit the transmission tender awards, the Union budget outlay and bank credit to industry. Furthest right, at three quarters, is peak power demand and shortfall: the earliest warning on the chart.

Use it as a reading order. Each quarter, start from the right: is power demand still outrunning supply, are tenders still being awarded, did the budget hold its capital line? Then check the one-quarter dots for margin pressure. The left-hand dot tells you what is already in the numbers.

Below the chart sits the rule and its three signs.

  • Inflows outgrowing sales: a tick, noted as yes but slowing.
  • Long equipment lead times: a tick, transformers still rationed.
  • Private capex joining: a cross, patchy and tariff-clouded.

Two of three means mid-cycle, which matches the clock on the fifth card.

Finally, the call box: the headline, three points behind it and what would change it. Treat those last three as alerts. Two straight quarters of falling inflows at the large names, transformer lead times shortening as new global capacity arrives, or a sharp cut in government capex would each send the call back for a rethink.
